chunks.title: Who I am
chunks.text: I'm Muneeb Ahmad, an AI engineer based in Lahore, Pakistan (UTC+5). I fix support chatbots that give customers wrong answers, and more generally chatbots, RAG assistants and AI agents that worked in the demo and broke in production. I measure before I touch anything and hand back before and after numbers, so you can check the fix instead of trusting me.

chunks.title: What this chat is
chunks.text: This chat is an AI version of me, not me typing. It answers only from notes I wrote and reviewed about my work, and it tells you when something isn't in them. Every sentence it shows has been checked against those notes first. The real me answers in Upwork Messages.
ask: Are you a real person or an AI?
Am I talking to a bot?

chunks.title: Background
chunks.text: I have four years of building and running Python, FastAPI and Docker services in production, with CI/CD. My AI work is RAG systems with real evaluation harnesses (golden sets, LLM-as-judge, faithfulness gates, Langfuse tracing), LangGraph agents, MCP servers and OWASP-LLM guardrails. I work in React and Node when the fix reaches the frontend.

chunks.title: Why check me instead of believing me
chunks.text: My public repository holds 13 measured experiments on one RAG pipeline, with the failures kept in. Sample sizes are stated, and the fixes that did not work are still there. I also build a small working demo before applying to a job, so a client can try the hard part before hiring me. You don't have to take my word for any of it.

chunks.title: Where I am on Upwork
chunks.text: I'm new on Upwork. My profile carries the Rising Talent badge and has no completed Upwork contracts yet, so instead of reviews I show measured work you can check: the public evaluation harness, three live demos, and this page.

chunks.title: What my public work is and isn't
chunks.text: My public repository is applied LLM and RAG engineering, built on top of backend work. It is not deep learning research or MLOps at scale, and I don't claim it is.

chunks.title: Languages
chunks.text: I speak English fluently, and Urdu is my native language.

chunks.title: Skills
chunks.text: Retrieval augmented generation, AI agent development, AI evaluation, evaluation harness design, large language models, hallucination mitigation, LangChain, LangGraph, Model Context Protocol (MCP), Python, FastAPI, API integration, AI model integration, vector databases, the Claude API, the OpenAI API, software debugging, Docker, LLM prompt engineering and generative AI.

chunks.title: My method, in four steps
chunks.text:
1. I reproduce the failure with a test set built from your real questions, not toy examples.
2. I measure before touching anything: answer accuracy, faithfulness to your documents, cost per query.
3. I fix the root cause (retrieval, chunking, prompts, tool calls, guardrails), not the symptom.
4. I re-run the same tests and give you the numbers, plus tracing so you can see what the model does in production after I'm gone.

chunks.title: How I would fix a support chatbot that gives wrong answers
chunks.text: For a support chatbot that gives customers wrong answers, I do three things. First, I take 20 to 30 of your real customer questions and count how many come back wrong today. Second, I fix the biggest cause, which is usually retrieval, the instructions, or a missing rule for when not to answer. Third, I run the same questions again and hand you the before and after table. The number tells you it's done, not me.
ask: How would you fix my support bot?
Our chatbot gives customers wrong answers
How do you fix a chatbot that hallucinates?

chunks.title: What I fix
chunks.text: Chatbots and RAG assistants that hallucinate or give wrong answers. Retrieval that pulls the wrong documents, or none. Agents that loop, stall, or break on real user input. LLM apps with runaway token costs, no error handling, or no visibility into what the model is doing. Half-finished integrations of OpenAI, Anthropic or open-source models into an existing Python backend.
ask: What kind of problems do you fix?

chunks.title: How an engagement starts
chunks.text: I start with a fixed-price diagnostic and a written findings report. You decide whether to continue from there, and you keep the report whether or not you hire me for the fix.

chunks.title: Why I measure first
chunks.text: None of the failures in my repository were found by reading code. They were found by building something that produces a number, then trying to make the number move. The order is measure, instrument, fix, measure again, and keep the runs that proved me wrong.

chunks.title: Building a new assistant
chunks.text: I also build small assistants on a client's own documents when done can be measured as right answers out of a set of their real questions. The tests exist from the first day, the way they do in my demos.

chunks.title: What I will not claim
chunks.text: A finding I cannot evidence is labelled a hypothesis, never presented as a cause. Stand-in data is called stand-in data. If a result contradicts what I predicted, the prediction stays in the write-up next to the result.

chunks.title: The public evaluation harness
chunks.text: My public repository holds 13 experiments on a single RAG pipeline. Each one asks a question that can be answered with a number and records the answer it actually got. I built one evaluation harness, rag_eval.py, 2,183 lines, and then spent thirteen sessions trying to break the pipeline it measures. Five of the thirteen sessions ended by disproving what I set out to prove. Total measured API spend across every experiment is $4.95.
ask: Tell me about your evaluation harness

chunks.title: The pipeline I measured
chunks.text: The pipeline: a corpus of 21 markdown files (712 KB), a chunker, the bge-small-en-v1.5 encoder, cosine top-k retrieval, a cross-encoder reranker with a pool of 20, a context builder that wraps every chunk in a per-request delimiter, a generator with a hardened system prompt, an agent loop gated behind a trigger, a segregated LLM judge, a citation validator with 19 unit tests, and Langfuse tracing.

chunks.title: The golden set and trap set
chunks.text: The golden set has 50 hand-written questions with keyword relevance rules. A separate trap set has 5 questions the corpus provably cannot answer, used to measure hallucination. A check command validates both before any run, because a question that matches zero chunks scores zero forever.

chunks.title: Experiment 01: chunking
chunks.text: Question: chunk size or encoder, which lever matters? At n=20 the encoder looked like the lever: bge-small over minilm gave +0.128 MRR. Re-run at n=50 on 18 September 2026, the same swap was +0.037, below the repository's own noise bar, so I withdrew the conclusion. I keep both runs side by side because that replication is the finding.

chunks.title: Experiment 04: reading the chunks by hand
chunks.text: Question: where does the keyword ruler disagree with a human reader? I read the retrieved chunks by hand, and that overturned my own earlier verdict: the overfitting miss was a ranking problem, not a coverage problem. That is what sent experiment 06 at a cross encoder rather than at a smaller chunk size.

chunks.title: Experiment 05: heading-aware chunking
chunks.text: Question: does splitting on headings rescue a known miss? No. The target chunk fell from full-corpus rank 8 to rank 67. Cleaner chunks helped 66 competitors more than they helped the target.

chunks.title: Experiment 06: reranking
chunks.text: Question: can a cross encoder rescue the two retrieval misses? One of two. The LSTM question flipped to a hit at a pool of 20. The overfitting question stayed a miss at every pool size from 5 to 30, so it was a scoring decision, not a recall problem.

chunks.title: Experiment 07: generation cost and latency
chunks.text: Question: what does an answer cost and how long does it take? $0.002174 per query and 2.1 seconds mean latency, measured per query.

chunks.title: Experiment 08: RAG versus fine-tuning
chunks.text: Question: which tool fits which problem? I diagnosed four scenarios as a knowledge problem or a behaviour problem and wrote the break-even out: a saving of about $72.47 a day means a small-model fine-tune pays back in days.

chunks.title: Experiment 09: stopping hallucination
chunks.text: Question: will the pipeline hallucinate on questions the corpus cannot answer? The prompt I had been shipping hallucinated on 15 of 15 trap runs. A better prompt alone took it to 0 of 15. Faithfulness went from 3.90 to 4.80, and groundedness from 66.9% to 95.6%.

chunks.title: Experiment 10: tracing refusals
chunks.text: Question: can I see refusals in production telemetry? A boolean score on every trace span. Traps abstained 5 of 5, golden questions 1 of 20. The single false abstention traced back to one chunk out of 734, so it was a chunking defect rather than a timid model.

chunks.title: Experiment 11: the agent loop
chunks.text: Question: is a search loop worth the money? Four of my five preregistered hypotheses were wrong. The loop fired on 2 questions in 20, with zero false fires, at 1.32 times the cost. Verdict: ship it behind a trigger, not by default.

chunks.title: Experiment 12: prompt injection
chunks.text: Question: what happens if someone writes into my corpus? 1,820 bytes of hostile text, 0.255% of the corpus, and the agent obeyed 8 of 18 runs. My own faithfulness judge scored the most successful attack 5 out of 5, fully grounded, three times out of three. The guard agreed with the attacker.

chunks.title: Experiment 12: the defence
chunks.text: The fix was a per-request random delimiter around every retrieved chunk, plus three lines telling the model that delimited text is data, not instructions. Obedience fell from 8 of 18 to 1 of 18, at 1.68 times the cost and no measured quality loss. A payload that only lies, giving no order, still gets through, and I wrote that up too.

chunks.title: Experiment 13: citation validation
chunks.text: Question: does forcing citations stop the attack? No. It caught none of the eight attacks that landed, because the attacker's method is to make the citation true. Segregating the judge did work: correct answers wrongly punished went from 4 to 0. The validator has 19 unit tests.

chunks.title: Experiment 14: an MCP server
chunks.text: Question: can I serve the retriever over MCP? Yes: an MCP server over stdio, built to the 2026-07-28 spec on mcp 2.0.0, verified three ways, including Claude Code discovering and calling it unprompted. Then I attacked it: a poisoned tool description got 0 of 3 compliance but 1 of 3 contamination.

chunks.title: Experiment 15: LangGraph durability
chunks.text: Question: does LangGraph durability survive a crash? Only on a flag that is not the default. With durability set to async, a kill -9 lost a model call I had already paid for. Setting it to sync fixes it.

chunks.title: What the experiments taught me
chunks.text: It invents answers the documents cannot support. It does whatever is written in its context. The guardrail you trust most can be the one that fails. It can quietly lose paid work when a process dies. Each of these was found by making a number move, not by reading the code.

chunks.title: Why I build demos
chunks.text: I build a small working demo before applying to a job, so a client can try the hard part of their own project before hiring me. Each demo runs in the browser with stand-in data, is built from the job post and not from the client's code, and says so on the page.

chunks.title: Demo: an AI assistant that knows when not to use AI
chunks.text: An assistant that sends prices to plain code, answers policy questions from documents with a citation, and declines what the documents don't cover. Real Python runs in the browser. With its safeguards on it passes 12 of 12 stand-in edge cases; with every safeguard switched off, the same code passes 4 of 12. It ships with 16 passing tests.

chunks.title: Demo: an inquiry agent with guardrails
chunks.text: An inquiry desk that answers customers from an approved fact sheet, fills a lead sheet, and sends discounts, refunds and custom quotes to the owner with a draft ready instead of promising them. You press play and watch it handle a morning of 12 stand-in inquiries. The approval routing is plain code in front of the model, so a model mistake cannot send a promise nobody approved.

chunks.title: Demo: a booking service that can't double-book
chunks.text: A meeting-room booking service with the hard part working: two people pressing Book at the same moment. It stages the race between the usual first version and mine, and checks 5 edge cases live. In Postgres the database itself refuses overlapping bookings with an exclusion constraint.

chunks.title: Reliability diagnostic (Project Catalog)
chunks.text: A written reliability diagnostic of your LLM, RAG or AI agent app. Starter, $95 in 2 days: I reproduce one failure you already see and send a 1 to 2 page write-up with the cause, the evidence and the smallest fix. Standard, $240 in 3 days: up to 8 failures across the whole request path, a prioritised 6 to 10 page report and a 30-minute call. Advanced, $480 in 7 days: adds an evaluation set of 25 to 50 real questions, a scoring script, and the top fix implemented and re-measured.

chunks.title: Prompt-injection test (Project Catalog)
chunks.text: Your RAG or AI agent tested for prompt injection, with the numbers. Starter, $120 in 3 days: a threat model and one working indirect injection against your own content. Standard, $320 in 5 days: 6 or more payloads over multiple runs, a measured obedience rate, and a check of whether your own guardrail can be fooled. Advanced, $640 in 10 days: the defence implemented and the whole suite re-run, with a before and after table.

chunks.text: The way to reach me is Upwork: send me a message there, or book the consultation from my profile. There is no email or phone number on this page on purpose. Upwork asks that we talk on the platform before a contract, and I keep to that.

chunks.title: What I don't take
chunks.text: I don't take no-code agent builders (GoHighLevel, n8n, Zapier, Voiceflow), voice-AI telephony, or mobile-first apps. I would be learning on your time.

chunks.title: Access and confidentiality
chunks.text: I never need production credentials. A staging copy, a repository, or an endpoint with a test key is enough. I work inside your repository or a private copy, I don't reuse your data, and I'm happy to sign an NDA through Upwork before starting.

chunks.title: Guarantees
chunks.text: I can't guarantee a system is safe afterwards, and I'd be wary of anyone who does. On my own pipeline the defence took obedience from 8 of 18 to 1 of 18, and one attack still worked. I show you what is still open rather than hide it.

chunks.title: If I can't reproduce the failure
chunks.text: If I can't reproduce a failure, the report says so, shows what I tried, and names the logging you would need to catch it next time.

chunks.title: What this chat answers
chunks.text: I keep this chat to professional questions: my work, my method, my experiments, my demos, what I offer, and how to hire me. Personal questions, opinions on news or politics, and general-knowledge questions are outside it.

chunks.title: When something isn't in my notes
chunks.text: If something isn't in my notes, I say so rather than guess. The real me answers on Upwork, so that is the place for anything this chat can't cover.

chunks.title: How this chat works
chunks.text: An open model, Llama 3.1 8B, writes the answer on Cloudflare's free tier, behind a small proxy that checks every request. It only sees the notes retrieved for your question. Before you see anything, every sentence is checked against those notes: the numbers, the names and the words have to be there. If a check fails, you get my notes verbatim instead. Nothing you type is stored.

chunks.title: The guardrails on this chat
chunks.text: A topic gate decides what the chat will answer before any model is called. A separate classifier looks for prompt injection. Requests are rate limited and need a bot check. The last line of defence is not the prompt: it is the verifier that rejects any sentence my notes don't support. That is the same lesson as my experiment 12, where the guard I trusted agreed with the attacker.
ask: What guardrails does this chat have?

chunks.text: I fix support chatbots that give customers wrong answers, so this page is one of them: a support chatbot about me that answers only from my notes and says no to everything else. Try to make it say something that isn't true.

chunks.text: No. A staging copy, a repository, or an endpoint with a test key is enough. I never need production credentials.

chunks.text: The Starter diagnostic takes 2 days, the Standard 3 days, and the Advanced, with an evaluation set and the first fix re-measured, 7 days.

chunks.title: Our chatbot gives customers wrong answers. Can you help?
chunks.text: Yes, that is the problem I specialise in. I count how many of your real customer questions come back wrong today, fix the biggest cause, and re-run the same questions so you get a before and after table.

chunks.title: Can you stop hallucinations completely?
chunks.text: I can measure them and push them down, and show you the number. On my own pipeline a better prompt took hallucinations on trap questions from 15 of 15 to 0 of 15. I won't promise zero on your system before I've measured it.

chunks.title: Can you test our assistant for prompt injection?
chunks.text: Yes. I build working attacks against a copy of your own content, measure how often the model obeys them, check whether your guardrail can be fooled too, and rank the fixes. I never attack a production system.

chunks.title: Can you build an evaluation set for us?
chunks.text: Yes. I build a golden set from your real questions, a scoring script, and a gate that fails when a change makes answers worse, the way my public harness works.

chunks.title: Can you build a RAG assistant from scratch?
chunks.text: Yes, when it's a small assistant on your own documents and done can be measured as right answers out of a set of your real questions. The tests exist from the first day.

chunks.title: Do you build AI agents?
chunks.text: Yes, in code: LangGraph agents and MCP servers. I don't build on no-code agent platforms.

chunks.title: Should we fine-tune instead?
chunks.text: My experiment 08 is about exactly that choice: whether a problem is missing knowledge or wrong behaviour, and when a fine-tune pays back. For wrong answers in a support bot, the cause is usually retrieval or instructions, not the model's knowledge, so I measure first.

chunks.title: Can you reduce our LLM costs?
chunks.text: I measure cost per query first, the way I did in experiment 07 ($0.002174 per query, 2.1 seconds), and then look for the cause of the spend. I won't quote a saving before I've measured your system.
